# Computational Resources and Tools {#sec-book-appendix-b}


::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## What This Appendix Covers {.unnumbered}

This appendix catalogues resources used in the book: environments and libraries (@sec-appb-environment, @sec-appb-libraries), datasets (@sec-appb-datasets), pretrained models (@sec-appb-models) and community infrastructure (@sec-appb-community). Reproduction notes follow in @sec-appb-reproducing. Entries refer to the sources and revisions checked; newer and unlisted resources need their own verification.
:::

The resources include rule-based tools from Apertium and HFST, corpora from OPUS and Common Voice, models from the Hugging Face Hub, and language-specific datasets from groups such as ISSAI and SIGTURK. This appendix gives starting points; the task chapters describe the relevant releases and limitations.


## Environment Setup {#sec-appb-environment}

### Tested Profiles and Installation

Use separate environments for HFST/toolkit work, transformer experiments and Omnilingual ASR. The book's runs used Python 3.11 to 3.13, with packages varying by chapter. Each run records Python and package versions and downloaded-file SHA-256 hashes. Reuse those records when reproducing a result, and check other platform or package combinations before relying on them.

For a fresh environment, choose a supported Python/runtime and the platform-specific PyTorch installation from its official instructions, then install the pinned direct dependencies in `code/common/requirements-tested.txt`. That file records the checked package versions; it is not a complete cross-platform lock or evidence of a clean install on every OS. Save the resolved environment for a published experiment.

Install only the toolkit extras needed by the chosen example. HFST availability and native dependencies differ by platform; a Windows environment may need WSL for those tools. The Omnilingual wrapper's environment is separate from the Whisper recipe in @sec-book-11-speech-technologies. Do not install conflicting speech stacks into an existing working text environment.

Memory and runtime depend on the exact configuration, so measure them on the planned run; each exercise README records the runtime of the book's run. The exercises run on a CPU; the procedure-only fine-tuning recipes are faster on a GPU.

## Key Libraries and Frameworks {#sec-appb-libraries}

### Hugging Face Ecosystem

The Hugging Face ecosystem is the primary software infrastructure used throughout this book. Four libraries are central.

**`transformers`** provides a unified API for loading, fine-tuning, and running pretrained models. Models are identified by a Hub ID string (e.g., `dbmdz/bert-base-turkish-cased`); the appropriate model class and input conventions depend on whether the task uses an encoder, a causal language model or a sequence-to-sequence model. Pin the revision of every checkpoint, as the exercises do; a newly added task head is random until trained.

**`datasets`** loads corpora and benchmarks from the Hugging Face Hub or from local files, with streaming for large datasets. The book's exercises instead read most datasets from commit-pinned GitHub files and check their SHA-256 hashes (for KazNERD and KyrgyzNER, see @sec-book-09-sequence-labeling), so that a rerun uses exactly the same release.

**`peft`** implements parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods including LoRA and QLoRA, which reduce the memory needed to adapt large models. Use the complete XLM-R sequence-classification recipe in @sec-ch12-hands-on. Target names are architecture-specific, and a new classifier head must be trainable and saved with its adapter. Copying `q_proj/v_proj` from a decoder into a BERT example is not a valid universal setup.

**`evaluate`** wraps standard metrics such as `seqeval` for BIO entity spans, `sacrebleu` and `chrf` for machine translation and `rouge` for summarisation. Feature and exact-bundle accuracy for morphology are computed by the book's own code (@sec-book-15-evaluation-benchmarks); report the metric signature with every score.

The Hugging Face Hub at [huggingface.co](https://huggingface.co) hosts models, datasets and spaces relevant to Turkic NLP. Language tags (e.g. `kk` or `kaz` for Kazakh) are self-reported metadata: a tag search can miss resources and count copies, so record the query and date, as the resource audit in @sec-ch17-hands-on does.

### TurkicNLP Toolkit

The TurkicNLP toolkit [@hakimov2025turkicnlp] provides one pipeline for 24 Turkic languages, with interchangeable rule-based, finite-state (Apertium), per-language neural (Stanza), and multilingual neural (Glot500) backends, plus script detection, transliteration, Common Turkic Script (CTS) conversion, language identification (GlotLID), morpheme segmentation, and NLLB-based embeddings and translation.

- **GitHub**: [github.com/turkic-nlp/turkicnlp](https://github.com/turkic-nlp/turkicnlp)
- **Installation**: `pip install turkicnlp` (extras such as `turkicnlp[hfst]` add heavier backends)
- **Languages**: 24 (coverage per component differs; see the model catalogue)
- **Processors**: `tokenize`, `mwt`, `morph`, `morph_neural`, `pos`, `feats`, `lemma`, `depparse`, `ner`, `embeddings`, `translate`, `sentiment`, `spellcheck`, `sp_tokenize`, `asr`
- **Other entry points**: `LanguageDetection`, `SpeechRecognizer`, `MorphemeTokenizer`, `Transliterator`, `turkicnlp.llm.ask`, `list_processors`, `list_asr_languages`
- **LLM backends**: `morph`, `ner`, `translate`, `sentiment` and `spellcheck` can use any LLM (vLLM, Ollama, OpenAI, Claude, or a local Hugging Face model) for all 24 languages
- **Licences**: the library is Apache-2.0; Apertium transducers (GPL-3.0) and NLLB weights (CC-BY-NC-4.0) are downloaded separately

```python
# pip install "turkicnlp[stanza]==0.5.0"   # list_processors works without it; loading Stanza models needs it
import turkicnlp

print(sorted(turkicnlp.list_processors("kaz")))   # what the catalog offers for Kazakh
turkicnlp.download("kaz", processors=["tokenize", "morph"])
kz = turkicnlp.Pipeline("kaz", processors=["tokenize", "morph"])
doc = kz("Үйлерімізден өте алыс кеткенбіз.")
for word in doc.words:
    print(word.text, word.lemma, word.upos, word.feats)
print(doc._processor_log)                          # which backend produced what
print(doc.to_conllu())
```

Three behaviours are worth knowing. **Field ownership**: when several processors provide the same field, the last one in the pipeline owns it, and the others' values are kept in `word._provenance`. **Script bridging**: input in a script without models (Kazakh Latin, Uzbek Cyrillic) is transliterated, processed, and mapped back to the original text. **Batching**: `nlp.batch(texts, batch_size=32)` hands whole batches to the neural and LLM backends.

### Apertium

Apertium [@forcada2011apertium; @khanna2021apertium] is an open-source rule-based machine translation and morphological analysis platform. For Turkic NLP, its primary value is the collection of finite-state morphological analysers for 20+ Turkic languages, whose coverage and ambiguity should be evaluated against independent gold data.

- **Website**: [apertium.org](https://apertium.org)
- **GitHub**: [github.com/apertium](https://github.com/apertium)
- **Turkic language modules**: [github.com/apertium/apertium-tur](https://github.com/apertium/apertium-tur) (Turkish), [github.com/apertium/apertium-kaz](https://github.com/apertium/apertium-kaz) (Kazakh), and equivalents for other languages

@sec-rbmt-apertium gives a dated inventory of Apertium translation pairs and their development stages. Check the selected pair's release and supported direction before use; a repository listing does not guarantee support in both directions.

### HFST (Helsinki Finite-State Toolkit)

HFST [@linden2011hfst] is a toolkit for compiling and running finite-state transducers. The Apertium Turkic analysers used in this book are compiled with HFST; Apertium also supports other finite-state toolchains.

- **Website**: [hfst.github.io](http://hfst.github.io)
- **Installation**: `pip install hfst` (Python bindings) or system packages

HFST supports the standard finite-state operations (composition, intersection, minimisation); @sec-book-06-finite-state-morphology shows how to load and query the Apertium transducers with its Python bindings.

### Stanza (Stanford NLP)

Stanza [@qi2020stanza] provides neural NLP pipelines for tokenisation, POS tagging, morphological analysis, and dependency parsing. Its 1.11.0 model catalogue has models for five Turkic languages with UD data: Turkish, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Uyghur and Ottoman Turkish (later catalogues add Uzbek; @sec-book-08-syntax-ud); TurkicNLP adds Stanza models for Azerbaijani, Uzbek, Turkmen, Tatar, and Bashkir.

TurkicNLP exposes Stanza backends through its pipeline (@sec-ch08-hands-on). Check the catalogue for the requested language and processor: a parsing model does not imply that a dedicated NER model is available.

Use Stanza 1.11 (`pip install "turkicnlp[stanza]"` enforces `stanza>=1.8,<1.12`): the custom Azerbaijani, Uzbek, Turkmen, Tatar and Bashkir models were trained with it, and newer Stanza versions fail to load their parsers.

The measured Stanza baselines, including the caveat on the Kazakh replay score, are in @sec-book-08-syntax-ud. For other languages, TurkicNLP's multilingual Glot500 tagger and parser and its Apertium backend are the alternatives.

### Zemberek-NLP (Turkish)

Zemberek [@akin2007zemberek] is an open-source Java library for Turkish morphological analysis, disambiguation, tokenisation, spell-checking and normalisation ([github.com/ahmetaa/zemberek-nlp](https://github.com/ahmetaa/zemberek-nlp)); community Python wrappers exist. Verify the maintained implementation and evaluate it on the intended domain.

: Parallel corpora covering Turkic languages {#tbl-parallel-corpora}

The **TIL corpus** [@mirzakhalov2021large] provides parallel data for 22 Turkic languages; release-specific counts, directions and split-overlap cautions are discussed in @sec-book-10-machine-translation. **FLORES-200** provides the same evaluation sentences for the eleven Turkic varieties in NLLB-200 and is one possible MT evaluation source, provided language coverage, contamination and domain fit are checked.

### Monolingual Corpora

| Corpus | Language | Approx. Size | URL |
|--------|----------|:------------:|-----|
| HPLT v3.0 | many, incl. 11 Turkic subsets | per-language sizes in @sec-corpora-inventory | hplt-project.org |
| FineWeb2 | many, incl. Turkic | per-language sizes in @sec-corpora-inventory | huggingface.co/datasets/HuggingFaceFW/fineweb-2 |

| Turkish National Corpus | tur | 50M words (2012 description) | [Corpus description](https://aclanthology.org/L12-1590/) |

: Monolingual corpora for Turkic languages {#tbl-mono-corpora}

The **Turkish National Corpus (TNC)** [@aksan2012tnc] was designed as a balanced, general-purpose corpus of 50 million words. This is the size reported in the 2012 description. **HPLT**, **FineWeb2** and **CulturaX** are automatically labelled web collections. Their per-language sizes differ substantially; @sec-book-04-corpora-at-scale compares their releases and explains how to audit a subset before use.

### Treebanks

UD 2.17 has treebanks for Turkish, Ottoman Turkish, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Uzbek, Uyghur, Tatar, Azerbaijani, Sakha (UD: Yakut) and Old Turkic (UD: Old Turkish), plus Turkish–German and Turkish–English code-switching treebanks (@sec-book-08-syntax-ud, @tbl-turkish-treebanks and @tbl-other-treebanks). They provide reference annotations for tokenisation, POS tagging, morphological features and dependency structure in CoNLL-U format. Annotation methods and quality vary by treebank; check the release documentation and the examples in @sec-book-08-syntax-ud.

- **Download**: [universaldependencies.org](https://universaldependencies.org) (all treebanks, versioned releases)
- **Parallel UD-Turkic sentences**: [github.com/ud-turkic/parallel](https://github.com/ud-turkic/parallel) [@eslami2025parallel]
- **Format**: CoNLL-U (tab-separated syntactic-word records, with additional records for multiword tokens and empty nodes)
- **Python loading**: `pip install conllu`

In the audited official UD 2.17 inventory, languages without a dedicated released treebank include Turkmen, Bashkir, Chuvash, Crimean Tatar, Gagauz, Karakalpak, Kumyk, Nogai, Karachay-Balkar, and all Siberian Turkic languages except Sakha.

| Dataset | Language | Entity Types | Source | Reference |
|---------|----------|:------------:|----------------|-----------|
| KazNERD | Kazakh | 25 classes; 112,702 sentences | github.com/IS2AI/KazNERD | @yeshpanov2022kaznerd |
| KyrgyzNER | Kyrgyz | 27 classes; 7,033 training and 3,867 test sentences | github.com/Akyl-AI/KyrgyzNER | @turatali2025kyrgyzner |

: Named entity recognition datasets for Turkic languages {#tbl-ner-datasets}

**KazNERD** reports 112,702 sentences from Kazakh television news, with 136,333 annotations in 25 classes [@yeshpanov2022kaznerd]. It supplies the NER examples in @sec-book-09-sequence-labeling. **WikiANN** derives silver-standard annotations from Wikipedia in many languages. Its original publication and later releases differ in coverage; use the pinned configurations in that chapter and assess label quality for the chosen language and task.

**TUMLU** [@isbarov2025tumlu] lists Azerbaijani, Crimean Tatar, Karakalpak, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Tatar, Turkish, Uyghur and Uzbek, with school questions in 11 subjects; its conflicting language counts require release-specific checks (@sec-book-15-evaluation-benchmarks). **Kardeş-NLU** [@senel2024kardes] evaluates cross-lingual NLU for five Turkic languages with Turkish as a high-resource relative. **Mukayese** [@safaya2022mukayese] is a multi-task benchmark suite for Turkish.

## Pretrained Models {#sec-appb-models}

### Verified Configurations

{{< include ../tables/tbl-verified-models/output.md >}}

The table counts base-model parameters from pinned configurations on a meta device, without downloading weights. BERTurk vocabulary variants have different embedding sizes; XLM-R base is not the 125M-parameter monolingual RoBERTa base. A task head changes the count. The CSV preserves model class, source URL, revision and licence metadata.

### Additional Models

Glot500, NLLB, BERTbek, TURNA, KAZ-LLM and Sherkala are discussed with their publications and task results in @sec-book-07-neural-morphology, @sec-book-10-machine-translation and @sec-book-12-pretrained-lms. Use each experiment's pinned checkpoint and verify any additional Hub release. Choose by measured performance and model purpose: NLLB is trained for translation, while base mT5 uses span-corruption pretraining. Instruction-following chat requires further adaptation or evaluation.

: Speech models for Turkic languages {#tbl-speech-models}

**Whisper** (OpenAI) covers seven Turkic languages (tr, az, uz, kk, tt, tk, ba) but not Kyrgyz or Uyghur. **TurkicASR** [@mussakhojayeva2023turkicasr] covers Azerbaijani, Bashkir, Chuvash, Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Sakha, Tatar, Turkish, Uyghur, and Uzbek; **TurkicTTS** [@yeshpanov2023turkictts] synthesises Turkic languages zero-shot from a Kazakh-trained model (@sec-book-11-speech-technologies).


## Community and Infrastructure {#sec-appb-community}

The organisations behind most of these resources (Apertium, SIGTURK, ISSAI, Universal Dependencies, Turkic Interlingua, the UD-Turkic group, TurkLang and the Turkic Academy) are described in @sec-institutions. Two practical points for contributors:

- **Universal Dependencies** publishes two releases a year; new treebanks are submitted through the UD GitHub organisation, and language-specific guidelines are in the UD documentation. For a language without a treebank, see @sec-build-treebank.
- **Apertium** modules are separate GitHub repositories (`apertium-kaz`, `apertium-kir`, `apertium-nog`, …) documented on [wiki.apertium.org](https://wiki.apertium.org); extending an existing module is the route described in @sec-bootstrapping.


## Reproducing Results from This Book {#sec-appb-reproducing}

### Local Reproduction Manifest

The code is organised by chapter: `code/ch04-corpus/`, `code/ch05-ambiguity/`, `code/ch06-toy-fst/`, `code/ch07-neural/`, `code/ch09-ner/`, `code/ch10-mt/`, `code/ch11-speech/`, `code/ch12-classify/`, `code/ch13-retrieval/`, `code/ch14-generation/`, `code/ch15-tumlu/`, `code/ch16-transfer/` and `code/ch17-resources/`. Shared helpers, the mechanical checks and the tested package versions are in `code/common/`, whose README documents inputs, commands, outputs and limits for classification, speech, TUMLU, corpus auditing, retrieval, transfer and resource observations. The exercise notebooks are in `exercises/`.

Run `python code/common/check.py` in the recorded test environment. This checks fixtures, tiny models and artefact reload; it does not reproduce pretrained-model task accuracy. Full data/model downloads, dataset access conditions and independent human labels are separate prerequisites. Code-block extraction alone is not an adequate end-to-end reproduction test.

### Setting Up Chapter by Chapter

The reading routes in the Preface give the order of chapters. Install only the extras a chapter uses, and keep the speech environment separate.
